messages.subject: inla.mesh.create.helper vs 2d
messages.subject_clean: inla.mesh.create.helper vs 2d
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I've been running INLA, creating the mesh through inla.mesh.create.helper with no issues.
The mesh looked fine and the analysis ran smooth. I now just wanted to play around with the mesh
so I tried using inla.mesh.2d (again) with the same exact parameters and it is just incredibly slow/not working.
I can create a mesh within maybe 5-10 seconds using inla.mesh.create.helper, with the 2d command it's been
over 2 hours already.
I'm just wondering where the issue lies here and if using the inla.mesh.create.helper is leaving something out and would
thus be false? I did read somewhere that the helper function is obsolete (a post from 2013). However, many other, more recent
examples use this function to create meshes.

mesh = inla.mesh.create.helper(points = locations, max.edge = c(0.02, 0.05), min.angle = c(21,21), cutoff = 0.005)

vs

bnd <- inla.nonconvex.hull(locations, convex= 0.12)
mesh = inla.mesh.2d(boundary = bnd, max.edge = c(0.02, 0.05), min.angle = c(21,21), cutoff = 0.005)

In short: can I use inla.mesh.create.helper to produce a quality mesh or am I loosing something?

Thanks already for any help or answers. I appreciate it!

Cheers,
Katrin

Based on some exploratory data analysis, I found that my smoothness parameter for the Matern covariance function is typically estimated above 40.  In the function inla.spde2.matern(), I have noticed that alpha has a restriction on the interval from 0 to 2.  Is there any way to increase this alpha value, or is it something that may be available in the future?  I realize increasing alpha results in less sparsity in Q thus longer computation times, but for my application I think the results would be more meaningful if I could set alpha higher to achieve smoother results.  Any insight or suggestions are much appreciated, thank you for your help!

Steve

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Selecting smoothness parameter alpha for the Matern cov fn
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Smoothness above around 4-5 is very hard to distinguish from infinity (which corresponds to a “squared exponential” covariance, so I wouldn’t hold too much weight on the value 40, much larger and much smaller values will produce very similar fields. But as you say, smoothness 1 (spde order 2) can be noticeably less smooth.
Due to the way inla is coded internally, the easiest way to access smoother spde model is to build your own precision matrix as part of an “rgeneric” model. That is how e.g. the “barrier model” has been implemented, and how we are working to get more general spatial-temporal models.  I think there are some rgeneric examples linked from r-inla.org <http://r-inla.org>. You can follow the Lindgren et al 2011 paper for the definition of the precision for the higher order models, and use inla.mesh.fem() to access the needed c0, g1, g2, g3, etc matrices.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
they are in the same scale as the linear predictor. the default for the
poisson is

y ~ Poisson(exp(lin.predictor))

yes, so if an estimate for the precision is 50 then an estimate for the
variance is 1/50 = 0.02. you can compute the posterior the variance if
you want to get it 'right'.

be aware, that for intrinsic models, like default besag, rw1, rw2, this
does not correspond to the 'marginal precision' but a 'precision
parameter', as there is a buildt in scale in these models depending on
the dimension, locations and the graph. well, adding scale.model=TRUE
in the f(), will remove this effect and make the precision also the
marginal precision (in the sense that is defined with intrinsic
models). We recommend adding scale.model=TRUE by default.

Best
H

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] modeling the difference between two Binomials?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] modeling the difference between two Binomials?
messages.body_plain:
Thanks so much!

We are doing a meta-analysis with interest in heterogeneity of effects by randomized experiment j and population subgroup g (a cross-classification of 3 factors: g1, g2, g3). Outcomes are binary.

Let Y_jgt = number of successes in experiment j, subgroup g, treatment group t, out of a sample size of n_jgt.

Y_jgt ~ Binomial(n_jgt, p_jgt)

logit(p_jgt) ~ Normal(a_0 + a_g1 + a_g2 + a_g3 + a_j + b_0*t + b_g1 * t + b_g2 * t + b_g3 * t + b_j * t, sigma)

priors:
a_g1 ~ Normal(0, sigma_1)

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] "random effects" interactions?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] "random effects" interactions?
messages.body_plain:
INLA does not have any concept of 'nested random effects' hence you're
free to do what you want.

with

y ~ f(g1, model="iid") + f(g2, model="iid")

you're just specifying which components in 'f(g1...)' and 'f(g2...)'
that goes into the linear predictor for y'

if 'u' is the first term, 'v' the second, then with normal data,

y[1] ~ N(  intercept + u[g1[1]] + v[g2[1]], ..)
y[2] ~ N(  intercept + u[g1[2]] + v[g2[2]], ..)
y[3] ~ N(  intercept + u[g1[3]] + v[g2[3]], ..)

etc.

> g1 = as.factor(c("a", "b", "a", "a"))
> g2 = as.factor(c(1,2,2,1))
> g1g2 = as.factor(paste(g1,g2,sep=""))
> cbind(g1,g2,g1g2)
     g1 g2 g1g2
[1,]  1  1    1
[2,]  2  2    3
[3,]  1  2    2
[4,]  1  1    1
> g1g2
[1] a1 b2 a2 a1
Levels: a1 a2 b2

then its just

formula = y ~ 1 + f(g1) + f(g2) + f(g1g2)

there is a backdoor-option to define joint priors for the
hyperparameters, if you *really* need it..

H

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Exponential Prior for GMRF parameters
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

This appendix is written from the perspective of dividing the total randomness or variation of the data into
- likelihood randomness (iid, cannot be "modelled")
- spatial randomness (spatial random effect)
- structured randomness (fixed effects etc)

You can think of it as decomposing a signal into modelled randomness and residuals.

The idea presented here is that the amount of "randomness" (or variation) you want to include in the spatial term should have the same penalty no matter how much you have "already included".

Best,
Haakon

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

The inla.mesh.projector objects are really only descriptors of mapping
between mesh basis function weights and evaluations of the resulting
functions at some given locations, so don't make sense as sp or sf
objects. The inla.mesh.project output is the vector of evaluated
function values at the given locations, so one can for example do
this:

# mesh = your mesh
# nodeval = the function values at the mesh nodes (e.g. from inla output)
# projloc = Where you want to evaluate

proj <- inla.mesh.projector(mesh, projloc)
spvalues <- SpatialPointsDataFrame(
  projloc,
  data = data.frame(values = inla.mesh.project(proj, field = nodevalues)))

There's also ggplot2 support that uses sp internally in the inlabru package:

library(inlabru)
ggplot()+gg(mesh) # Just plot the mesh
ggplot()+gg(mesh,color = mesh$loc[,1]) # Plot a function with given
mesh node weights

The latter uses inla.spde.make.A and SpatialPixels internally, via the
user-visible function inlabru::pixels()
Part of the pixels() code:
  px <- pixels(data, nx = nx, ny = ny)
  A <- INLA::inla.spde.make.A(data, px)
  px$color <- as.vector(A %*% color)
# This results in a SpatialPixelsDataFrame

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Is it possible to fit a model with an error term on original scale (eps_I) and one on log scale (eps) with INLA? And how is such a model specified with the call to the inla function of RInla?

y = eta + eps_N
log(eta) = X beta + eps
eps_N ~ N(0,tau_N)
eps ~ N(0, tau)

Background:
I want to analyze data with a stochastic component at log-scale, i.e. lognormal, but measurement error on original scale is assumed normal.
In the studied soil CO2 efflux data, total error increases with response magnitude, but there are scatter and negative observations for small responses.
I want to disentangle the two sources.

In the real data the "X beta" part is more complex involves a smoother with time and random effects by location that also slowly change with time. This is hard to explore with MCMC and I hoped I could use INLA.

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Yes, this should be possible, at least in the type of structure you describe, where the log-link applies to the whole linear predictor except for the final Gaussian error term. You will need to tell inla to use a log-link with the Gaussian observation family instead of the default identity-link. You can think of the observation model as being

Y~ N(exp(eta), tau_N)
where eta is the linear model
eta=X beta + eps

(In INLA terminology, eta is always the linear predictor)

(For more complex nonlinear constructions the inlabru package allows more general predictor expressions, but in your case plain inla should be fine)

Finn
